previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type II diabetes, Chagas-related cardiomyopathy, and a history of coronary artery bypass grafting was admitted for evaluation of fever and found to have a worsening pleural effusion. He had recently undergone a failed AV fistula attempt and presented with malaise, chills, and cough. Workup included thoracentesis and pleuroscopic biopsy, which showed exudative fluid with active pleuritis but no malignancy or infection. He underwent thoracoscopy and pleurodesis to prevent reaccumulation. Post-procedure, he developed bradycardia and hyperkalemia, likely vagally mediated, which resolved with insulin therapy and hemodialysis. His fever resolved, attributed to a viral syndrome. He was discharged home with a PleurX catheter for outpatient drainage, visiting nurse support, and follow-up appointments.

radiology_notes.text:
RADIOGRAPHS OF THE PELVIS, LEFT HIP AND SACRUM 

HISTORY:  Sacral, pelvic and left buttock pain after a fall.  Question
fracture.

COMPARISONS:  Abdominal radiograph is available from ___, and
prior CT of the pelvis is available from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Pelvis, single AP view, with two views of the left hip and two
lateral views of the sacrum.

FINDINGS: There is no evidence for fracture, dislocation, or bone destruction.
Degenerative changes are suspected at the lower lumbar facets.  The hip joint
spaces are mildly narrowed with small marginal osteophytes.  Vascular
calcifications are widespread.  Surgical clips project over the left upper
medial thigh.  

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of fracture.

CHEST RADIOGRAPHS

HISTORY:  Fever and cough.

COMPARISONS:  Radiographs from ___ CT from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Chest, AP and lateral.

FINDINGS:  The patient is status post coronary artery bypass graft surgery.  A
dialysis catheter again terminates in the upper atrium.  The heart is mildly
enlarged.  The mediastinal and hilar contours appear unchanged.  There are
similar patchy linear opacities in the left mid lung as well as right lung
opacities with a moderate pleural effusion in the right costophrenic angle
that may be loculated to some degree.  A posterior wedge-like opacity is
nonspecific but suggests additional loculated fluid as a likely etiology or
round atelectasis.  This opacity seems to correspond to perhaps increased
fluid associated with left lower lobe atelectasis or scarring seen on the
prior CT.  Comparing the right-sided pleural effusion directly to the most
recent prior study, there has been no definite change allowing for differences
in technique.

IMPRESSION:  Essentially stable appearance of the chest including moderate
right-sided pleural effusion with suspected loculation and associated opacity,
probably compatible with atelectasis.

INDICATION:  ___ male with end-stage renal disease and recent pleural
effusion, now with high fever and cough.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images through the chest were acquired without
intravenous contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformatted images were reviewed.

FINDINGS:  There has been interval placement of a right pleural catheter.  New
loculations of air within the small right pleural effusion are seen.  Adjacent
atelectasis is present.  There is slightly increased fluid or thickening of
the minor fissure.  High attenuation along the right pleura suggests prior
pleurodesis.  Left basilar atelectasis or scarring and left upper lobe
atelectasis or scarring is again noted.  Right upper lobe atelectasis or
scarring is also again noted.  Decreased attenuation of the right upper lung
parenchyma compared to the left is unchanged.  Evaluation of the heart and
great vessels is limited in the absence of intravenous contrast. No
pericardial effusion is detected.  Heart size is enlarged.  Post-CABG changes
and sternotomy wires are again noted.  A large-bore central catheter is again
noted terminating in the right atrium.  Prominent mediastinal lymph nodes are
present, without pathologic enlargement.  The visualized portion of the
thyroid is homogeneous.

IMPRESSION:  Interval development of locules of air within the right pleural
effusion; this may be secondary to interval placement of a pleural catheter
with introduction of air, but loculated infection cannot be excluded.
